subjects.displayTitle: The Greatest Name: remembrance, recognition, and renewal
subjects.introduction: A name seen in a room can awaken a joy that remains for years. From that intimate moment, these readings open onto the Greatest Name as invocation, symbol, and a way of speaking about revelation itself. They associate its remembrance with recognition of Baha’u’llah, the awakening of spiritual life, and steadfastness amid difficulty. The ringstone explanation distinguishes the worlds of God, revelation, and creation, while prayers give voice to longing for protection, understanding, healing, and nearness. The Qur’an’s invitation to call upon God through the beautiful names offers a comparative setting for reflection on sacred naming [1]. Connected subjects explore Baha’u’llah, daily recitation, the Word of God, and the power of speech. Together the passages invite attention to how words become meaningful in a life: through understanding, affection, repeated remembrance, and the actions that remembrance inspires.
subjects.arc: Begin with joy and daily remembrance, explore meanings and symbols, follow the language of hidden and manifest revelation, then read prayers for renewal and the call to steadfast action.

subjects.displayTitle: East and West: learning to meet as one human family
subjects.introduction: Every place is east of somewhere and west of somewhere else. That observation opens a compilation in which geographical distance becomes an invitation to friendship, mutual assistance, and shared learning. Letters, visits, schools, translations, marriages, and gatherings give practical form to the hope that East and West might embrace. The passages also preserve historical accounts of religion, material progress, domination, and cultural misunderstanding. Their broad regional comparisons belong to particular speakers and settings; the aspiration to one human family invites thoughtful examination of those categories. The Qur’an’s account of peoples knowing one another offers a comparative perspective on diversity and relationship [1]. Neighboring subjects consider community building, Iran, material and spiritual civilization, and both praise and criticism of Eastern and Western cultures. Together they ask how encounter might replace inherited suspicion with reciprocal responsibility and the joy of learning from others.
subjects.arc: Begin with the relativity of East and West and universal belonging, make encounter tangible through friendship and communication, examine reciprocal learning and historical tensions, then return to peace and shared service.

subjects.displayTitle: Science and religion: inquiry with the whole mind
subjects.introduction: What would it mean to test even a cherished teaching with the powers of reason? This compilation begins with that invitation and follows it into the relationship between scientific discovery, religious understanding, and human flourishing. Images of two wings, twin lights, and a shared center suggest mutual support, while the repeated criticism of superstition makes harmony a demanding practice. The readings also ask what knowledge serves: technical achievement needs moral direction, and spiritual aspiration needs disciplined investigation. Neighboring subjects explore the mind’s powers, the limits of our ways of knowing, and the difference between insight and inherited opinion. Emerson’s reflections on thought and devotion offer a comparison with their own philosophical commitments. The closing letters invite patient engagement with ambiguity, distinguish inquiry from institutional endorsement of treatments, and leave readers with the task of building a civilization in which learning and conscience develop together.
subjects.arc: Begin with the invitation to test the speaker’s words, examine the unity of truth and the work of reason, explore interpretation and changing knowledge, then consider moral purpose and the closing letters on patient inquiry.
